api/Axiam.Sdk.Amqp.AxiamAmqpConsumer.htm.summary: Class AxiamAmqpConsumer Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Amqp Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll AMQP event consumer: verify-before-handler HMAC gate plus the sdks/CONTRACT.md §8 ack/nack matrix, built on RabbitMQ.Client 7.x's async consumer API with automatic connection/topology recovery enabled (D-11). StartAsync(string, string, byte[], Func<byte[], CancellationToken, Task>, ILogger?, TimeSpan?, CancellationToken) NEVER hands an unverified delivery to the caller-supplied handler — Verify(byte[], byte[]) runs first, and the handler call site is structurally unreachable until it returns true. The remaining outcomes follow the exact §8 decision matrix: HMAC verification fails → BasicNackAsync(requeue: false) + a security-event log entry that never contains the received or expected HMAC value; the handler is never invoked. HMAC verifies but the NEW-4 replay-protection gate (ReplayGuard) rejects the delivery — key_version below MinKeyVersion, a stale/future issued_at, or a replayed nonce — → BasicNackAsync(requeue: false) + a security-event log entry; the handler is never invoked. Handler returns normally → BasicAckAsync. Handler throws PoisonMessageException (poison message) → BasicNackAsync(requeue: false). Handler throws any other exception (transient/retryable) → BasicNackAsync(requeue: true). public sealed class AxiamAmqpConsumer : IAsyncDisposable Inheritance object AxiamAmqpConsumer Implements IAsyncDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Fields DefaultNetworkRecoveryInterval Default network-recovery interval applied to the connection factory. public static readonly TimeSpan DefaultNetworkRecoveryInterval Field Value TimeSpan DefaultPrefetchCount Default QoS prefetch count. public const ushort DefaultPrefetchCount = 10 Field Value ushort Methods DisposeAsync() Performs application-defined tasks associated with freeing, releasing, or resetting unmanaged resources asynchronously. public ValueTask DisposeAsync() Returns ValueTask A task that represents the asynchronous dispose operation. StartAsync(string, string, byte[], Func<byte[], CancellationToken, Task>, ILogger?, TimeSpan?, CancellationToken) Connects to amqpUri, opens a channel with automatic recovery enabled, and registers an RabbitMQ.Client.Events.AsyncEventingBasicConsumer on queue that verifies every delivery's HMAC-SHA256 signature (§8, via Verify(byte[], byte[])) BEFORE handler is invoked, then applies the §8 ack/nack matrix documented on this class. public Task StartAsync(string amqpUri, string queue, byte[] signingKey, Func<byte[], CancellationToken, Task> handler, ILogger? logger = null, TimeSpan? replaySkew = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters amqpUri string The AMQP connection URI. queue string The queue name to consume from. signingKey byte[] The per-tenant AMQP HMAC signing secret (§8.1 — obtain from the AXIAM management API; never hardcode). handler Func<byte[], CancellationToken, Task> Invoked ONLY after HMAC verification AND the NEW-4 replay-protection gate (ReplayGuard) both succeed. Throw PoisonMessageException to drop a message without requeue; any other exception is treated as transient and requeues. logger ILogger Receives the §8.4 security event on HMAC verification (or NEW-4 replay-protection) failure; the event never contains the HMAC, nonce, or issued_at value. Defaults to a silent no-op logger. replaySkew TimeSpan? The NEW-4 freshness window applied to each delivery's issued_at field (also sets the nonce dedup store's TTL, 2×replaySkew). Defaults to DefaultSkew (±5 minutes) when null or non-positive. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token for connection/channel setup and for every ack/nack call issued by the registered consumer. Returns Task

api/Axiam.Sdk.Amqp.Hmac.html.summary: Class Hmac Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Amqp Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll HMAC-SHA256 verify-before-handler primitive for inbound AMQP messages (sdks/CONTRACT.md §8, D-11). Canonicalization is wire/insertion-order preserving, NEVER alphabetically sorted. The canonical Rust signer (crates/axiam-amqp/src/messages.rs's sign_payload) signs the serde_json struct-declaration-order serialization of the message body (with hmac_signature absent). JsonObject is backed by an ordered dictionary and preserves insertion order from parsing by default — Remove(string) mutates that same ordered map in place, preserving the relative order of all remaining keys. This is the single load-bearing property of this class: do NOT introduce an alphabetized copy, OrderBy/Sort, or a POCO deserialize-then-reserialize round-trip here — any of those would silently reorder fields and break every cross-language HMAC verification. public static class Hmac Inheritance object Hmac Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Methods Verify(byte[], byte[]) Returns true iff body's hmac_signature field matches HMAC-SHA256(signingKey, canonical_json_of(body_without_hmac_signature)), computed via a constant-time comparison. Never throws: malformed JSON, a missing/null signature, non-hex signature text, or a wrong-length signature all verify as false — matching §8.3's strict-mode default that rejects (rather than silently accepts) an unparseable or absent signature. public static bool Verify(byte[] signingKey, byte[] body) Parameters signingKey byte[] The per-tenant AMQP HMAC signing secret (§8.1). body byte[] The raw AMQP delivery body bytes. Returns bool true if the signature is valid, false otherwise.

api/Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.AxiamAuthMiddle.title: Class AxiamAuthMiddleware | AXIAM .NET SDK
api/Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.AxiamAuthMiddle.summary: Class AxiamAuthMiddleware Namespace Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore Assembly Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.dll ASP.NET Core authentication middleware (D-06, CONTRACT.md §10 "ASP.NET Core" row: app.UseMiddleware<AxiamAuthMiddleware>() in Program.cs). Mirrors sdks/java/.../spring/AxiamAuthenticationFilter.java's authoritative sequence (extract → verify → exp-check → cross-tenant-check → inject-identity → 401 JSON on failure), adapted to ASP.NET Core's ClaimsPrincipal/User integration point — the direct analog of Java D-14's Spring SecurityContext integration. public sealed class AxiamAuthMiddleware Inheritance object AxiamAuthMiddleware Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Security-critical invariants (T-21-17, T-21-19, T-21-20): When NO credential is presented at all, the request is passed through unauthenticated — the framework's own [Authorize]/authorization middleware 401s it (via AxiamAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler, registered by AddAxiamAspNetCore(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>)). This middleware never rejects a request for the mere absence of a token (Java filter lines 78-83 precedent) — doing so would incorrectly 401 public/anonymous endpoints that never carry a token at all. When a token IS presented, it is verified via the shared AxiamClient's internal JwksVerifier local fast path: alg-pinned Ed25519 signature check, THEN the mandatory post-signature tenant_id claim check (Pitfall 3 — the JWKS document is organization-wide, not tenant-scoped, so signature validity alone never implies tenant authorization). An explicit exp re-check is performed here too as defense in depth, mirroring the Java filter's lines 88-91 even though JwksVerifier.VerifyAsync already checks exp internally. User is rebuilt from scratch on every request from a fresh VerifyAsync call — it is NEVER cached beyond the current request, and never beyond the token's own remaining TTL (§10). Every failure path writes a standardized JSON body via WriteAsJsonAsync<TValue>(HttpResponse, TValue, CancellationToken) (System.Text.Json) — never manual string concatenation, so a message containing quotes/control characters can never produce malformed or injected JSON (PATTERNS.md "Standardized JSON error body"). CSRF (cookie double-submit, CONTRACT.md §3): when the credential was sourced from the axiam_access COOKIE (not the Authorization header) and the request method is state-changing (anything other than GET/HEAD/OPTIONS), this middleware additionally requires the X-CSRF-Token request header to be present and equal (constant-time, FixedTimeEquals(ReadOnlySpan<byte>, ReadOnlySpan<byte>)) to the axiam_csrf cookie value, rejecting with 403 on mismatch/absence. Bearer-header requests are CSRF-immune by construction — a cross-site attacker cannot set arbitrary request headers — but a cookie automatically attached by the browser is not, and in any same-site deployment where axiam_access reaches this app, the non-httpOnly axiam_csrf cookie does too. This mirrors, locally, the same double-submit check the AXIAM server performs on its own endpoints (§3). Constructors AxiamAuthMiddleware(RequestDelegate) Constructs the middleware. api/Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.UmaChallenger.h.title: Class UmaChallenger | AXIAM .NET SDK
api/Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.UmaChallenger.h.summary: Class UmaChallenger Namespace Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore Assembly Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.dll A configured WWW-Authenticate: UMA challenge emitter (CONTRACT.md §20.3, emit half). public sealed class UmaChallenger Inheritance object UmaChallenger Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Register one with AddAxiamUmaChallenge(IServiceCollection, UmaChallenger) and a [Authorize(Policy=…)] denial stops being a bare 403: AxiamPolicyHandler mints a fresh permission ticket for the action the caller lacked and AxiamAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler returns it in the header, so a UMA-aware client knows where to go for authority instead of only being told "no". Opt-in, and deliberately so. Emitting a challenge means minting a credential — a wire call to the Protection API, and a live ticket, produced on a path the caller did not explicitly request. A handler that did that on every denial by default would turn each unauthorized request into a Protection API call, which is a denial-of-service amplifier pointed at your own authorization server. So it happens only where an application registered one. Failure is not escalation. If minting fails — the PAT expired, the Protection API is down, the resource declares none of the requested scopes — the denial still surfaces as an ordinary 403 without a challenge. A caller who was going to be refused is refused either way; letting a Protection API outage turn a deny into a 503 would hand the outage a second consequence, and letting it turn into an allow would be a security bug. api/Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore.html.summary: Namespace Axiam.Sdk.AspNetCore Classes AxiamAccessAttribute Declarative, per-endpoint AXIAM authorization attribute (CONTRACT.md §11 require_access(action, resource[, scope]) — C# maps this to [AxiamAccess(...)]). Sugar over the existing "resource:action" policy string mechanism (AxiamPolicyProvider/AxiamPolicyHandler): this attribute serializes its Action/Resource/ Scope/ResourceRouteParam into a structured policy name ("axiam::<action>::<resource>::<scope>::<param>") that AxiamPolicyProvider recognizes and parses ALONGSIDE the legacy single-colon "resource:action" form (which remains fully supported — see its own remarks). Because this type derives from AuthorizeAttribute, it can be placed directly on a controller/action ([AxiamAccess("read", "documents")]) or passed to RequireAuthorization(IAuthorizeData) for minimal APIs — ASP.NET Core's own authorization pipeline combines it into a policy via Policy exactly like any other AuthorizeAttribute. AxiamAuthMiddleware ASP.NET Core authentication middleware (D-06, CONTRACT.md §10 "ASP.NET Core" row: app.UseMiddleware<AxiamAuthMiddleware>() in Program.cs). Mirrors sdks/java/.../spring/AxiamAuthenticationFilter.java's authoritative sequence (extract → verify → exp-check → cross-tenant-check → inject-identity → 401 JSON on failure), adapted to ASP.NET Core's ClaimsPrincipal/User integration point — the direct analog of Java D-14's Spring SecurityContext integration. AxiamAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler Custom IAuthorizationMiddlewareResultHandler that writes the standardized JSON error body (CONTRACT.md §10/§11, PATTERNS.md "Standardized JSON error body") for every authorization outcome: an unauthenticated result (401), a "lacks permission" result (403 — AxiamPolicyHandler left an AxiamRequirement unsatisfied, i.e. AuthzError), an unresolvable resource id (400 invalid_request, CONTRACT.md §11.2.3), and a transport failure while checking access (503 authz_unavailable, fail-closed per CONTRACT.md §11.2.5). On success, the pipeline continues exactly like the framework default. AxiamOidcLoginOptions Configures MapAxiamOidcLogin(IEndpointRouteBuilder, string, string, Action<AxiamOidcLoginOptions>)'s login-redirect and callback endpoints (CONTRACT.md §12). Both endpoints share one options value so the two routes of a login flow cannot drift apart (same redirect URI, same scope). AxiamOptions Typed Options-pattern configuration for AddAxiam(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>)/ AddAxiamAspNetCore(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>) (D-07). Configured via services.AddAxiamAspNetCore(options => { ... }) — properties are mutable (set, not init) because the .NET Options pattern configures an already-constructed instance through an Action<T> delegate. AxiamPolicyHandler Routes [Authorize(Policy="resource:action")] (e.g. "documents:read") into AxiamClient.Authz.CheckAccessAsync (D-08). No direct Spring analog — Spring's sibling SDK uses method-security annotations rather than an IAuthorizationHandler/policy-provider pair, so this is the most novel file in the phase (built from RESEARCH.md Pattern 5, reusing the AuthzError→403 JSON-body convention from AxiamAuthenticationFilter.java lines 102-111). AxiamPolicyProvider Builds an AuthorizationPolicy containing a single AxiamRequirement for either the structured policy name produced by AxiamAccessAttribute or the legacy policy name shaped "resource:action" (e.g. "documents:read") — the novel .NET-idiom file this phase introduces (D-08; no direct Spring/method-security equivalent, built from RESEARCH.md Pattern 5). Falls back to DefaultAuthorizationPolicyProvider for every other policy name, so consumer-defined policies (registered via the normal AddAuthorization(options => options.AddPolicy(...)) path) keep working completely unmodified. AxiamRequirement Authorization requirement carrying everything AxiamPolicyHandler needs to run a single AXIAM access check (CONTRACT.md §11): the resource/action halves (legacy "resource:action" policy-string form, e.g. "documents:read", or the structured AxiamAccessAttribute form — both funnel into this same type), plus the optional Scope and the ResourceRouteParam route value name used to resolve the target resource's UUID at request time. Built by AxiamPolicyProvider. OidcLoginEndpointExtensions ASP.NET Core minimal-API endpoints implementing "Login with AXIAM" (CONTRACT.md §12) — MapAxiamOidcLogin(IEndpointRouteBuilder, string, string, Action<AxiamOidcLoginOptions>) wires the login-redirect and callback endpoints into the existing middleware/DI pipeline, resolving the shared AxiamClient and IOidcStateStore singletons AddAxiam(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>)/AddAxiamAspNetCore(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>) register. ServiceCollectionExtensions IServiceCollection DI extensions (D-07): AddAxiam(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>) registers the typed AxiamOptions plus a single shared AxiamClient; AddAxiamAspNetCore(IServiceCollection, Action<AxiamOptions>) additionally wires the policy-based authorization surface (D-08). The raw app.UseMiddleware<AxiamAuthMiddleware>() form (CONTRACT.md §10) remains available and works with either registration path. UmaChallenger A configured WWW-Authenticate: UMA challenge emitter (CONTRACT.md §20.3, emit half).

api/Axiam.Sdk.Auth.DpopVerifier.html.summary: Class DpopVerifier Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Auth Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll DPoP proof verification — CONTRACT.md §21.7.2 (RFC 9449), contract 1.16. public static class DpopVerifier Inheritance object DpopVerifier Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The resource-server half of DPoP: given the DPoP header a caller presented, decide whether it proves possession for this request and this access token, and return the key thumbprint that VerifyTokenBinding(JsonElement, PresentedProofs) then matches against the token's cnf.jkt. Why this lives in the SDK. §21.7.2 is a ten-check list, and the contract is blunt about partial implementations: "Partial verification is worse than none, because it produces a guard that reports success." Nine of the ten look optional until someone builds an attack out of the one that was skipped, so they belong in one audited place rather than in every application guarding an endpoint. The two most often missing: typ — without pinning it to dpop+jwt, any other JWT signed by the same key (an access token, an ID token) is replayable as a proof; and ath — without it, a proof captured on one request can be re-aimed at a different token held by the same key. The algorithm comes from the key, never from the header. alg: none and RSA-public-key-as-HMAC-secret are the same bug wearing different clothes: the token told the verifier how to check the token. This class dispatches on the embedded key's own kty/crv, so an HMAC path is never reachable no matter what the header says. Ed25519 uses BouncyCastle for the same reason JwksVerifier does — .NET still ships no EdDSA. ES256 and PS256 use the platform's own ECDsa and RSA. Fields IatLeeway §21.7.2 check 7 — the iat acceptance window, applied in both directions. public static readonly TimeSpan IatLeeway Field Value TimeSpan Remarks RFC 9449 recommends a small window without fixing a number; 60 seconds is the contract's RECOMMENDED value. A named constant, because a bare 60 three call frames deep is a number nobody ever revisits. Methods AccessTokenHash(string) Compute the ath claim value for an access token — RFC 9449 §4.2. public static string AccessTokenHash(string accessToken) Parameters accessToken string The token as it arrived. Returns string The 43-character base64url hash. Remarks base64url-unpadded SHA-256 over the token's ASCII bytes, i.e. over the compact JWT string exactly as it travelled in the Authorization header, not over anything decoded out of it. CanonicalHtu(string) Reduce a URI to its htu comparison form — §21.7.2 check 6. public static string CanonicalHtu(string uri) Parameters uri string The URI to reduce. Returns string The same URI without its query string or fragment. Remarks Query and fragment removed, and nothing else. No case folding, no default-port elision, no percent-decoding, no trailing-slash fixing: a normalising comparison is precisely where two unequal URIs become equal, and an attacker who finds such a pair can aim a proof at an endpoint it was never minted for. ThumbprintS256(JsonElement) Compute the RFC 7638 SHA-256 thumbprint of a JWK — the jkt. public static string ThumbprintS256(JsonElement jwk) Parameters jwk JsonElement The public key to fingerprint. Returns string The 43-character base64url thumbprint. Remarks Only the members RFC 7638 names for the key type take part, serialised as compact JSON with lexicographically ordered keys. Members outside that set (kid, use, alg, x5c) are excluded by the spec, which is what makes the thumbprint stable across two encodings of the same key. Exceptions AuthError When the key type is unsupported or a member is missing. VerifyProof(string, DpopRequest, IJtiStore) Verify a DPoP proof against this request — all ten §21.7.2 checks. public static string VerifyProof(string proof, DpopVerifier.DpopRequest request, DpopVerifier.IJtiStore jtiStore) Parameters proof string The raw DPoP header value. request DpopVerifier.DpopRequest The method, URI and access token this proof must match. jtiStore DpopVerifier.IJtiStore The replay guard. Required — there is no default, because every default here is either a silent skip of replay protection or a per-process store masquerading as a global one. Returns string The proof key's jkt. Remarks Returns the proof key's RFC 7638 thumbprint (jkt) on success. Feed it to VerifyTokenBinding(JsonElement, PresentedProofs) as the DPoP half of PresentedProofs; returning it rather than true is deliberate, so the value a guard passes onward could only have come from a proof that actually verified. There is no "just check the signature" mode, because that is exactly the partial verification the contract calls worse than none. Exceptions AuthError On any failing check.

api/Axiam.Sdk.Auth.JwksVerifier.html.title: Class JwksVerifier | AXIAM .NET SDK
api/Axiam.Sdk.Auth.JwksVerifier.html.summary: Class JwksVerifier Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Auth Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll Local EdDSA (Ed25519) JWKS verification (D-02, CONTRACT.md §10 local-verification fast path). .NET has no native Ed25519/EdDSA support anywhere in System.Security.Cryptography (confirmed research finding — dotnet/runtime #14741/#63174 remain unimplemented through .NET 10 GA), so this class uses BouncyCastle.Cryptography's Org.BouncyCastle.Crypto.Signers.Ed25519Signer / Org.BouncyCastle.Crypto.Parameters.Ed25519PublicKeyParameters directly — the single, well-vetted, verify-only crypto dependency D-02 permits. public sealed class JwksVerifier Inheritance object JwksVerifier Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) applies the COMPLETE CONTRACT.md §10.1 "minimum local-verification set", every rule of which fails closed. This SDK uses NO JWT library: there is no System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt, JwtSecurityTokenHandler or TokenValidationParameters anywhere in the dependency graph (.NET ships no Ed25519 primitive, so the JOSE processing is hand-rolled over BouncyCastle). Every rule below is therefore enforced explicitly here rather than delegated to a library whose defaults would need auditing. signature — alg is pinned to "EdDSA" and checked BEFORE any key (kid) lookup, so alg: none and HS-family confusion are rejected without ever consulting a key. The token's own header never selects its verifier. exp — REQUIRED. A token carrying no exp, or an exp that is not a JSON number, is rejected. An absent exp is a *permanent credential*, never "no expiry constraint" — treating it as the latter is the SEC-080 defect. nbf — honoured when present; an nbf in the future is rejected. An absent nbf is valid. tenant_id — REQUIRED and asserted against the caller-supplied expected tenant, AFTER signature verification succeeds. An absent claim, or an empty expected tenant, fails closed. The JWKS document is organization-wide, not tenant-scoped, so a valid signature alone never implies tenant authorization (Pitfall 3 — independently confirmed by every sibling SDK). iss — checked only when this verifier was constructed with an expected issuer (see ExpectedIssuer). Unset by default. aud — checked only when this verifier was constructed with an expected audience (see ExpectedAudience). Unset by default. Accepts the single-string and array forms RFC 7519 permits. clock skew — ClockSkewLeeway, a named 60-second constant applied to rules 2 and 3. It is deliberately NOT operator-configurable. VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) NEVER throws for attacker-controlled input — every failure mode (bad alg, unknown kid, tampered/invalid signature, wrong tenant, missing/expired/ non-numeric exp, future nbf, issuer/audience mismatch, malformed/ non-base64/truncated token) returns null. This matches the AMQP HMAC verifier's fail-closed convention (Amqp/Hmac.cs). Constructors JwksVerifier(HttpClient, Uri, TimeSpan, string?, string?) public JwksVerifier(HttpClient httpClient, Uri baseUrl, TimeSpan cacheTtl, string? expectedIssuer = null, string? expectedAudience = null) Parameters httpClient HttpClient Used only to fetch the JWKS document; ownership stays with the caller. baseUrl Uri The AXIAM server base URL; the JWKS path is resolved relative to it. cacheTtl TimeSpan How long a fetched JWKS document is trusted before a refetch is forced. expectedIssuer string The iss claim value this verifier requires (CONTRACT.md §10.1 rule 5). CONDITIONAL: null/empty (the default) means no issuer check is performed at all; once supplied, a token whose iss differs — or which carries no iss — is rejected. There is no default value and no hardcoded AXIAM issuer. expectedAudience string The aud value this verifier requires (CONTRACT.md §10.1 rule 6). CONDITIONAL: null/empty (the default) means no audience check is performed at all; once supplied, a token whose aud does not contain it — including a token with no aud at all — is rejected. A verifier fronting a user-facing resource server should generally expect axiam:user. Fields ClockSkewLeeway The single, named, bounded clock-skew allowance applied to the exp and nbf checks (CONTRACT.md §10.1 rule 7 — RECOMMENDED 60 s). public static readonly TimeSpan ClockSkewLeeway Field Value TimeSpan Remarks Deliberately a const and not an option: §10.1 requires the leeway be "a named constant, not an inline literal" and forbids it being "operator-configurable to an unbounded value". Exposing it as a knob is the exact failure mode the rule exists to prevent. Methods CertificateThumbprintS256(byte[]) Compute the RFC 8705 §3.1 x5t#S256 thumbprint of a DER client certificate: base64url-encoded SHA-256, without padding. public static string CertificateThumbprintS256(byte[] der) Parameters der byte[] The DER encoding of the peer's leaf certificate — under ASP.NET Core, HttpContext.Connection.ClientCertificate?.RawData. Returns string Remarks Unpadded is not a style choice — RFC 7515 §2 defines base64url in JOSE as omitting =, and a padded value will not compare equal to what AXIAM put in the token. A well-formed value is exactly 43 characters. VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) Verifies jwt against the COMPLETE CONTRACT.md §10.1 minimum local-verification set: EdDSA-pinned signature against the cached (or freshly fetched) org-wide JWKS, a REQUIRED exp, an nbf honoured when present, a mandatory tenant_id asserted against expectedTenantId, and the conditional iss/aud checks when this verifier was configured with an expectation — all under ClockSkewLeeway. Returns the decoded claims payload on success; returns null for ANY failure. Never throws on malformed or attacker-controlled input — see the type-level remarks for the fail-closed contract. public Task<JsonElement?> VerifyAsync(string jwt, string expectedTenantId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters jwt string expectedTenantId string cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<JsonElement?> VerifyCertificateBinding(JsonElement, string?) CONTRACT.md §10.1 rule 9 — enforce a token's sender constraint against the certificate the caller presented on this connection (RFC 8705 §3 / RFC 7800, contract 1.15). public static bool VerifyCertificateBinding(JsonElement claims, string? presentedThumbprint) Parameters claims JsonElement The verified claims returned by VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken). presentedThumbprint string RFC 8705 §3.1 x5t#S256 of the peer certificate on this connection, or null when the connection carries none. Returns bool true when the constraint is satisfied or absent; otherwise false. Remarks A token carrying cnf is not a bearer token. Accepting one without proving the caller holds the named key converts it straight back into one, discarding the whole protection the operator turned on — which is why this is a rule and not a recommendation. The four cases: cnf absent anything → true (an ordinary bearer token) x5t#S256 equal → true x5t#S256 different, or no certificate → false cnf present with no x5t#S256 anything → false The first row is why adopting this rule breaks nothing: an unbound token is still accepted whether or not a certificate is present. Rule 9 constrains tokens that claim a constraint; it does not make certificates mandatory. The last row is the one that is easy to get wrong. A cnf naming a confirmation method this SDK cannot check — a DPoP jkt, say — is an unverifiable constraint, never no constraint. Read the other way, a sender-constrained token silently degrades to a bearer token the day a newer AXIAM issues a confirmation this SDK predates. The thumbprint must come from the transport. Under ASP.NET Core that is HttpContext.Connection.ClientCertificate passed through CertificateThumbprintS256(byte[]), or a value a trusted terminating proxy forwarded over a channel your application controls. Never from a caller-settable request header: a forgeable input makes the whole mechanism decorative. VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) deliberately does not apply this rule — it has no transport to ask. A resource server accepting bound tokens must call both. VerifyTokenBinding(JsonElement, PresentedProofs) CONTRACT.md §10.1 rule 9 in full — enforce a token's sender constraint against every proof the caller presented (contract 1.16). public static bool VerifyTokenBinding(JsonElement claims, PresentedProofs proofs) Parameters claims JsonElement The verified claims returned by VerifyAsync(string, string, CancellationToken). proofs PresentedProofs What the caller proved on this connection and request. Returns bool true when the token may be accepted; otherwise false. Remarks This is the complete rule, and the one to use unless your transport genuinely cannot produce a DPoP thumbprint. The ten cases: token's cnf certificate DPoP result absent anything anything true x5t#S256 equal ignored true x5t#S256 different ignored false x5t#S256 null ignored false jkt ignored equal true jkt ignored different false jkt ignored null false both equal equal true both wrong/missing — false present, names neither anything anything false Two rows carry the weight. Both named is a conjunction: an operator who turned on two constraints asked for two, and satisfying the more convenient one is not compliance. Names neither is a refusal: a confirmation this SDK cannot interpret is an unverifiable constraint, and reading it as "unconstrained" is the exact downgrade rule 9 exists to prevent. That includes an empty cnf, which is also how proto3 delivers an empty CnfClaim over gRPC (§10.3 rule 3).

Two invariants are normative: Single-use: ConsumeAsync(string, CancellationToken) MUST return the entry AND delete it atomically, so a replayed callback cannot reuse a state. Expiry: an entry older than the store's TTL (10 minutes, at most — MaxTtl) MUST NOT be returned. Methods ConsumeAsync(string, CancellationToken) Atomically fetches AND REMOVES the entry for state. Returns null when the state is unknown, already consumed, or expired — three cases a caller MUST treat identically (as a failed login), because distinguishing them leaks whether a state ever existed. Constructors PrincipalScope(Guid?, Guid?, string?, Guid?, IReadOnlyList<Guid>?) Where the signed-in principal lives, and how far its roles reach — CONTRACT.md §5.2.2 and §5.2.3. public PrincipalScope(Guid? ActingTenantId = null, Guid? PrincipalTenantId = null, string? PrincipalTenantSlug = null, Guid? OrgId = null, IReadOnlyList<Guid>? ReachableTenantIds = null) Parameters ActingTenantId Guid? The tenant a request acts on — what the X-Axiam-Tenant header names. null when the server does not report it. PrincipalTenantId Guid? The tenant this principal's record lives in. The same value as ActingTenantId for every ordinary principal; the two diverge only once an organization-level principal selects another tenant to act on. This is where the account's own credentials belong, and what a §23 registration record for this account must be sealed against — see OpaqueEnrollmentForSelfAsync. Falls back to ActingTenantId when the server omits it, which is exactly right there: a server that cannot switch the acting tenant cannot make the two differ. PrincipalTenantSlug string Slug of PrincipalTenantId — "organization" for an organization-level principal; null when the server omits it. OrgId Guid? The caller's organization as a UUID (§5.2.2 rule 3). Read this rather than resolving a slug through GET /api/v1/organizations, which is super-admin-only and returns only the caller's own organization. ReachableTenantIds IReadOnlyList<Guid> The tenants this caller's roles reach, when they are narrowed (§5.2.3). null means unrestricted, which is both the common case and the only thing a server older than contract 1.35 can mean. A present list is a deliberately narrowed organization-level account: confine any tenant switch to it, because naming anything outside is refused at the header. Note the pairing with OrganizationLevel — a narrowed account still reports true there, so gating on that flag alone offers tenants the server will refuse. api/Axiam.Sdk.Auth.RefreshGuard.html.summary: Class RefreshGuard Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Auth Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll Single-flight token-refresh guard (D-10, CONTRACT.md §9): guarantees exactly one in-flight refresh call at a time, regardless of how many concurrent callers observe an expired/near-expiry access token. One instance is constructed per AxiamClient and shared across the REST and gRPC transports (D-10's "one guard across REST + gRPC on one client" requirement) — never a second instance per transport. public sealed class RefreshGuard : IDisposable Inheritance object RefreshGuard Implements IDisposable Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Correctness invariants (mirrors the Java sibling's RefreshGuard double-check- after-lock structure, adapted to SemaphoreSlim + Task<TResult> per CONTRACT.md §9's locked C# mechanism): The refresh delegate is deliberately awaited WHILE still holding the gate. This is what makes every concurrent caller queue on _gate.WaitAsync: the first caller to acquire the gate assigns _inFlight and awaits it before releasing; any caller that later acquires the gate finds _inFlight already completed (and, if still fresh, reuses it) instead of starting a redundant refresh (SC#2: 5 concurrent callers against an expired token ⇒ exactly 1 underlying refresh). On failure, _inFlight is cleared before rethrowing so a failed refresh is NEVER cached for the next caller — the next call always starts a fresh refresh attempt (§9.3: no retry loop inside the guard itself; the caller must re-authenticate from scratch). A subsequent call reuses an already-completed result only when it is still fresh (more than Axiam.Sdk.Auth.RefreshGuard.FreshnessMargin from expiry) — never a stale or faulted one. Constructors RefreshGuard(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TokenPair>>) Constructs a RefreshGuard around the given refresh delegate. public RefreshGuard(Func<CancellationToken, Task<TokenPair>> doRefresh) Parameters doRefresh Func<CancellationToken, Task<TokenPair>> Performs the actual token-refresh call (e.g. POST /api/v1/auth/refresh). Invoked at most once per in-flight refresh, regardless of how many concurrent callers invoke RefreshIfNeededAsync(CancellationToken) (§9 single-flight guarantee). Methods Dispose() Disposes the underlying SemaphoreSlim gate. public void Dispose() RefreshIfNeededAsync(CancellationToken) Called by both the reactive (401 / gRPC UNAUTHENTICATED) and proactive (near-expiry, JWKS-driven) refresh paths. Guarantees exactly one underlying refresh call regardless of how many callers invoke this concurrently. public Task<TokenPair> RefreshIfNeededAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<TokenPair>

LoginOpaqueAsync(string, char[], CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/opaque/login/start followed by /finish — OPAQUE login, RFC 9807 (CONTRACT.md §23). public Task<LoginResult> LoginOpaqueAsync(string usernameOrEmail, char[] password, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters usernameOrEmail string The username or email to authenticate with. password char[] The account password, as a char[] so the caller can clear it. This SDK clears every copy it makes but cannot clear the caller's array. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the exchange. Returns Task<LoginResult> The login outcome, exactly as LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) returns it. Remarks A sibling of LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken), not a replacement. It takes the same arguments and returns the same LoginResult, MFA branch included, so an application can switch a tenant to OPAQUE without touching its own code. What this does that LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) does not. The password never leaves this process. What crosses the wire is a blinded group element and a MAC, neither useful without the account's registration record and the tenant's OPRF seed — so a TLS-terminating proxy, an accidentally verbose request log, or a heap dump on the server cannot capture a plaintext password, because the server never has one. It also means a stolen record database is not offline-crackable on its own, which is the pre-computation resistance SRP could not offer. It does not protect against a compromised AXIAM server. One round trip, and no server-proof step. SRP had to guess a group before the server named one and restart the exchange if it guessed wrong; KE1 does not depend on the key-stretching function. And where the old §23.3 rule 6 had to mandate an M2 check in capitals — because skipping it kept only half the protocol — RFC 9807's AKE authenticates the server during the handshake, so opening KE2 is the proof that it holds the record. There is nothing left to skip. Cost. Runs the tenant's key-stretching function: Argon2id at 19 MiB and t=2 by default, which is tens to hundreds of milliseconds of CPU plus that memory, per attempt. That cost is the point — it is what makes a stolen record expensive to attack even by someone holding the OPRF seed. It runs on the thread pool rather than the caller's thread. When the credential check fails (§23.4 rule 7). Nothing is sent to login/finish — a KE2 that does not open is the authentication result — and what happens next depends only on the mode the login/start response carried, the tenant's opaque_mode: Under optional this method retries over LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken) with the same credentials before reporting anything, and returns that call's outcome. That is not belt-and-braces: optional is the mid-migration state, every account starts with no registration record and acquires one only when its password is next set, so treating the failed exchange as final would lock out every user of the tenant. Under required — and under an absent mode, which is a server older than the field, and any value this SDK does not recognise — the failure is an AuthError, the exchange is over, and nothing is retried. mode is not downgrade protection and this SDK does not present it as such: a hostile server that wanted the plaintext could answer 404 and get a fallback whatever it puts there. What closes that is the server refusing /auth/login under required, before it examines any credential. Exceptions NetworkError The tenant has OPAQUE disabled (the endpoint answers 404 — a property of the tenant, not of any user), libaxiam_opaque_ffi is not installed, or the server names a key-stretching function this SDK cannot ask for. Deliberately not AuthError: reporting a configuration gap as a credential failure would send a user off to reset a password that works, and would stop a caller falling back to LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken). AuthError A wrong password, an account that does not exist, or a server that does not hold the record — indistinguishable by design. Nothing is sent to login/finish in that case (§23.4 rule 7), and under a required tenant the exchange is over: a caller must not retry over LoginAsync(string, string, CancellationToken), which would hand the plaintext to an endpoint that just failed to prove itself and answers 403 opaque_required anyway. Under an optional tenant this method has already retried for you — see the remarks — so an AuthError from here is the password login's verdict. OPAQUE's envelope is sealed under the server's oblivious PRF, so there is no offline computation that produces a valid record. Note the parameters that are gone. There is no identity: the SRP version required the account's canonical username, and an email there produced a verifier no login could ever satisfy, whereas a record binds to a credential identifier the server chooses. And there is no group or KDF, because those come from the register/start response — a caller cannot pick a cost the server will not honour. The server reads it off the caller's own record, and this signature deliberately offers no way to name a different one: a parameter here would let an authenticated session mail an arbitrary address. Unlike ResendVerificationAsync(string, Guid, CancellationToken) this reports the outcome, because the caller is signed in to the account it is asking about and none of the outcomes tells it anything it did not already know: it returns when a token was minted and the mail enqueued; throws AuthzError on 409 (already verified, or the account is in a state that must not be sent a live token); and throws NetworkError on 429 (the daily resend limit). Only a 401 (client authentication failed) is an error, surfaced as OAuthProtocolError (§12.1 note 5, §12.3 rule 3); a 5xx is still a NetworkError — revoke returning void does not make a server error "success" (§12 T1 reference judgment call 20). SsoCompleteHandoffAsync(SsoCompleteHandoffParams, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/federation/handoff (CONTRACT.md §12.1) — redeem the single-use code the SAML and Apple flows deliver. public Task<SsoCompleteResult> SsoCompleteHandoffAsync(SsoCompleteHandoffParams @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params SsoCompleteHandoffParams The single-use handoff code. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task<SsoCompleteResult> The established session's identifiers and post-login destination. Remarks Those two protocols return cross-site, so the server cannot set SameSite=Strict session cookies on that response. It instead redirects the browser to the SPA's callback URL with a QueryParam query parameter; this call posts that code back same-origin, and this response is the one that carries the cookies (§12.1 note 12). The code is gone either way. It is valid for CodeTtlSeconds seconds and redeemable once. Redeem it from the same origin, immediately, and never retry a failed redemption: a 401 is terminal, and this method makes exactly one wire call so that it cannot become a retry by accident. Unknown, expired and already-redeemed all answer the same 401, deliberately. SsoCompleteOauth2Async(SsoCompleteOauth2Params, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/federation/oauth2/callback (CONTRACT.md §12.1) — step 2 of a plain-OAuth2 login. public Task<SsoCompleteResult> SsoCompleteOauth2Async(SsoCompleteOauth2Params @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params SsoCompleteOauth2Params The state and code the provider redirected back with. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task<SsoCompleteResult> The established session's identifiers and post-login destination. Remarks The session arrives as Set-Cookie (§12.1 note 6) through the same §4 cookie-jar path SsoCompleteAsync(SsoCompleteParams, CancellationToken) uses. §12.4 does not apply: an OAuth2 provider issues no ID token, so there is nothing to validate — the server authenticated the user by calling a configured userinfo endpoint with the access token it had just received (§12.1 note 11). SsoProvidersAsync(SsoProvidersParams?, CancellationToken) GET /api/v1/auth/federation/providers (CONTRACT.md §12.1) — which "Sign in with X" buttons to render for a workspace. public Task<FederationProviderList> SsoProvidersAsync(SsoProvidersParams? @params = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params SsoProvidersParams The workspace to list providers for; every field optional. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task<FederationProviderList> The providers to offer, possibly empty. Remarks The identifiers travel as query parameters; this is a GET and sends no body. The neighbouring start operations take the same four in a JSON body, and the two are one copy-paste apart. An empty list is a success. An unknown organization, a known one with nothing configured, and a request naming no workspace at all all answer 200 with an empty providers array (§12.1 note 9). Every one of them comes back as an ordinary result and nothing here synthesises a not-found: the endpoint is deliberately shaped so it cannot be used to enumerate organization or tenant slugs, and an SDK that reintroduced the distinction would reintroduce the oracle. A caller learns it named the workspace wrongly at the start operations, where every failure is a uniform 401. For the same reason this is the one federation operation that does not throw client-side when no workspace resolves. SsoStartAsync(SsoStartParams, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/federation/oidc/start (CONTRACT.md §12.1) — step 1 of first-time SSO against an UPSTREAM IdP. No JWT required. public Task<SsoStartResult> SsoStartAsync(SsoStartParams @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params SsoStartParams cancellationToken CancellationToken Returns Task<SsoStartResult> Remarks One tenant form (TenantId or TenantSlug) and one org form (OrgId or OrgSlug) must be resolvable, from the arguments or from this client's own construction options (§5.1). Redirect the browser to the returned AuthorizeUrl and round-trip State back into SsoCompleteAsync(SsoCompleteParams, CancellationToken) unmodified — the server keeps the nonce to itself (§12.1 note 7). Exceptions AuthError Tenant or organization context cannot be resolved — raised client-side with no wire call. SsoStartOauth2Async(SsoStartOauth2Params, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/federation/oauth2/start (CONTRACT.md §12.1) — step 1 of a login through a plain-OAuth2 upstream (GitHub, Facebook, generic_oauth2). public Task<SsoStartResult> SsoStartOauth2Async(SsoStartOauth2Params @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params SsoStartOauth2Params The federation config, redirect URI and workspace context. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task<SsoStartResult> The authorize URL and single-use state to round-trip. Remarks Call this, rather than SsoStartAsync(SsoStartParams, CancellationToken), exactly when the provider's protocol is OAuth2 (§12.1 note 10). The server refuses a mismatch with 400 rather than accepting it silently, so a client that assumes OIDC fails on every GitHub button. PKCE is mandatory on this path and is generated and stored server-side; nothing about it appears in the request or the response (§12.1 note 11). A 400 here can mean the RedirectUri is not on an origin the deployment accepts (§12.1 rule 12a). §2's 400 row makes that a NetworkError — this taxonomy's configuration/programming-error member, as distinct from the AuthError a 401 gets. It is not retried. TokenExchangeAsync(TokenExchangeParams, CancellationToken) POST /oauth2/token with the RFC 8693 grant (CONTRACT.md §15.1) — exchanges a token for a narrower one. public Task<ExchangedToken> TokenExchangeAsync(TokenExchangeParams @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params TokenExchangeParams The exchange arguments. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task<ExchangedToken> The issued, narrower token. Remarks What this method deliberately does not do: No default ActorToken (§15.2 rule 1). Passing null asks for impersonation; the SDK will not quietly reuse the client's own session token as the actor and turn that into a delegation. No retry or downgrade on unauthorized_client (rule 2) — a registration fact an operator must fix. No auto-narrowing on invalid_scope (rule 3). The server refuses instead of silently narrowing precisely so the caller finds out here. No adoption (rule 5), and no flag to enable it — a MUST NOT, where LoginClientCredentialsAsync(LoginClientCredentialsParams, CancellationToken) adoption is a MAY. A cross-tenant subject token answers invalid_grant, identically to an expired one. The SDK does not try to tell them apart (§15.3): the server collapses them because distinguishing them is a tenant-enumeration signal. Exceptions AuthError When no client secret is configured — client-side, with no wire call. Returns Task A task that completes when the resource set is gone. UmaExchangeTicketAsync(UmaExchangeTicketParams, CancellationToken) POST /oauth2/token with the uma-ticket grant (§20.1) — exchanges a ticket for an RPT. public Task<RequestingPartyToken> UmaExchangeTicketAsync(UmaExchangeTicketParams @params, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters params UmaExchangeTicketParams The ticket and the requesting party's token. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<RequestingPartyToken> The requesting party token. Remarks This method never retries. It issues exactly one request and is outside the §16 retry policy — not on 5xx, not on timeout, not on any transport failure (§20.2 rule 6). The ticket is consumed before the request is evaluated, so a failed exchange has already spent it: a retry cannot succeed, and under concurrency it is precisely the concurrent redemption a server whose storage engine this SDK cannot attest may admit twice (ilpanich/axiam#302). On failure, request a new ticket. What this method deliberately does not do: no default ClaimToken (rule 2) — it is required; no auto-narrowing on access_denied (rule 3); and no adoption (rule 4) — the RPT is the requesting party's token. The four ticket refusals — unknown, expired, already used, wrong client — all answer invalid_grant with one message. This SDK does not try to tell them apart (§20.4): the server collapses them so a caller cannot probe for live ticket handles. Returns Task<ResourceSet> The resource set. UmaRegisterResourceAsync(Sensitive<string>, ResourceSet, CancellationToken) POST /uma2/rreg/resource_set — registers a resource set (§20.1). public Task<ResourceSet> UmaRegisterResourceAsync(Sensitive<string> pat, ResourceSet resource, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters pat Sensitive<string> The Protection API Token. resource ResourceSet The resource set to register. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<ResourceSet> The registered set, carrying the server-assigned id. Remarks The pat is an explicit parameter, not this client's session. A Protection API Token must be a client-credentials token, because a ticket binds to the client_id that minted it — and this client's session is usually a user session, which names no client to bind to (§20.2 rule 1). UmaRequestTicketAsync(Sensitive<string>, IReadOnlyList<RequestedPermission>, CancellationToken) POST /uma2/perm — mints a permission ticket (§20.1). public Task<Sensitive<string>> UmaRequestTicketAsync(Sensitive<string> pat, IReadOnlyList<RequestedPermission> permissions, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters pat Sensitive<string> The Protection API Token. permissions IReadOnlyList<RequestedPermission> The pairs the resource server requires. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<Sensitive<string>> The opaque ticket. Remarks Scope names are validated here, against each resource's declared set. Asking for an undeclared scope is a 400, not a denial — the two are different failures, and this SDK surfaces the distinction the server draws rather than flattening it. UmaUpdateResourceAsync(Sensitive<string>, Guid, ResourceSet, CancellationToken) PUT /uma2/rreg/resource_set/{id} — replaces a resource set (§20.1). public Task<ResourceSet> UmaUpdateResourceAsync(Sensitive<string> pat, Guid resourceId, ResourceSet resource, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters pat Sensitive<string> The Protection API Token. resourceId Guid The resource set id. resource ResourceSet The new state. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancellation token. Returns Task<ResourceSet> The updated resource set. Remarks The scope list is replaced, not merged (§20.2 rule 8). Whatever resource.ResourceScopes holds becomes the complete declared set; omitting a scope removes it, which is how a resource server drops an authority. This method performs no read-before-write. VerifyEmailAsync(Sensitive<string>, Guid, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/verify-email (CONTRACT.md §25.1). public Task VerifyEmailAsync(Sensitive<string> token, Guid tenantId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) Parameters token Sensitive<string> The token from the verification mail. Build it with Wrap(T): a caller holding it as a bare string out of a mail link is the expected case, and wrapping a value can never leak it. tenantId Guid The tenant the account belongs to. cancellationToken CancellationToken Cancels the request. Returns Task Remarks Unauthenticated: a user whose address is unverified may have no session at all. tenantId is a body field here — this is not an /oauth2 endpoint, so §12.1 rule 2's query-parameter convention does not reach it. Returns Task<VerifiedLogoutToken> The sid/sub/jti the token names — never a bare bool, because the RP has to know which session to end. Dedup on jti yourself: delivery is at-least-once, and an SDK-side guard would have no durable store and would silently drop a real second logout after a restart. Remarks Every check exists because skipping it has a name: Signature, through the same §12.4 JWKS verifier the ID-token path uses — no second key-fetching path — which already pins EdDSA and requires a kid, so rotation cannot be defeated by omitting it. iss/aud: a token minted for another RP is not accepted here. events carries the back-channel-logout key. This is what distinguishes a logout token from an ID token; skipping it means accepting a replayed ID token as a logout instruction. nonce is absent. Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.4 forbids it, and its presence is the documented signature of an ID token being replayed. Rejected, not ignored. WebauthnDiscoverableFinishAsync(Sensitive<string>, string, CancellationToken) POST /api/v1/auth/webauthn/authenticate/discoverable/finish (CONTRACT.md §24.1). api/Axiam.Sdk.Core.ConfigClampedEvent.ht.summary: Class ConfigClampedEvent Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Core Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll Emitted at construction, once per caller-supplied setting the SDK clamped (CONTRACT.md §19.1, §19.2 rule 6). public sealed record ConfigClampedEvent : TelemetryEvent, IEquatable<TelemetryEvent>, IEquatable<ConfigClampedEvent> Inheritance object TelemetryEvent ConfigClampedEvent Implements IEquatable<TelemetryEvent> IEquatable<ConfigClampedEvent> Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks Two places in the contract require clamping rather than rejecting: §16.1's attempt cap, base delay and delay cap, and §17.1 rule 2's memo TTL. Both clamps are right — rejecting would break a caller whose configuration was merely optimistic, and honoring would let one client become the herd §16 exists to prevent. Doing it silently is the part that is wrong. An operator who set a 60-second memo TTL believes they have one. They have five seconds, and their staleness reasoning is off by a factor of twelve with nothing anywhere to say so. This event is what makes the clamp discoverable at the only moment it can be acted on. It is not emitted for a value already within its limit: an event that fires when nothing happened trains its reader to ignore it. Only SDK-internal code may construct an instance or read the wrapped value, via Axiam.Sdk.Core.Sensitive<T>.Reveal() — there is intentionally no public accessor. [JsonConverter(typeof(SensitiveJsonConverterFactory))] public readonly struct Sensitive<T> : IEquatable<Sensitive<T>> Type Parameters T Implements IEquatable<Sensitive<T>> Inherited Members object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) Remarks Per CONTRACT.md §7's C# row ("Struct with ToString() override returning "[SENSITIVE]""): ToString() and the paired SensitiveJsonConverter<T> both always emit the literal "[SENSITIVE]", regardless of the wrapped value. Equals(object?), Equals(T) and GetHashCode() are overridden to make a Sensitive<T> never value-comparable: Equals(object?) always returns false and GetHashCode() always returns a constant. This is deliberate — the default ValueType equality a struct would otherwise inherit performs a structural, field-by-field value comparison (via reflection, and, for a string field, a non-constant-time string.Equals), which would open a value-equality/timing side channel on the redacted value and would transitively leak into any compiler-synthesized record equality of a type that carries a Sensitive<T> field. Overriding to a constant closes that channel. Methods Equals(Sensitive<T>) A Sensitive<T> is intentionally never equal to anything — this suppresses the structural value comparison a struct would otherwise inherit from ValueType, which would be a value-equality/timing side channel on the wrapped secret. public bool Equals(Sensitive<T> other) Parameters other Sensitive<T> Returns bool Equals(object?) A Sensitive<T> is intentionally never equal to anything — this suppresses the structural value comparison a struct would otherwise inherit from ValueType, which would be a value-equality/timing side channel on the wrapped secret. public override bool Equals(object? obj) Parameters obj object Returns bool Expose() Returns the wrapped raw value. Public — this is the documented, deliberate resolution of the CONTRACT.md §7-vs-§12 conflict recorded for contract amendment T9: §7 says "the raw token string MUST NOT be exposed via any public getter API", written when every token lived only in the §4 httpOnly cookie jar; §12's OidcTokenSet (access_token/refresh_token/id_token) changes that premise by delivering tokens directly in the /oauth2/token JSON response body, so the calling application MUST be able to read them back out to persist, forward, or revoke them later — there is no cookie jar capturing them on its behalf. Call this only at the point of actually consuming the value; NEVER pass the result to a logging/tracing/diagnostic sink. ToString() and this type's JSON converter (SensitiveJsonConverter<T>) still always redact regardless of this accessor's existence — the redaction guarantee is unaffected, only the explicit, opt-in escape hatch changed from "does not exist" to "exists and is named for exactly this purpose". public T Expose() Returns T GetHashCode() Always returns a constant — never derives a hash from the wrapped value. public override int GetHashCode() Returns int ToString() Always returns the redacted literal, never the wrapped value. public override string ToString() Returns string Wrap(T) Wraps value in a Sensitive<T>. api/Axiam.Sdk.Management.ManagementManif.summary: Class ManagementManifest Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Management Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll A description of the tenant you want (CONTRACT.md §27.6). public sealed record ManagementManifest : IEquatable<ManagementManifest> Inheritance object ManagementManifest Implements IEquatable<ManagementManifest> Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks A manifest states what should exist. It is not a diff and not a migration: reconciling it against a tenant that already matches writes nothing, and reconciling it twice is the same as reconciling it once. What it never does is delete. Something the manifest does not mention is something the manifest has no opinion about, not something it wants gone (§27.6 rule 4) — otherwise adopting a manifest for five roles would be a request to remove every other role in the tenant. Keys (docs, editor, alice) are manifest-local and never reach the server. They exist so one entry can name another before either has an identifier, which is what lets a manifest be written before anything in it exists. [JsonConverter(typeof(WireEnumConverter<ActorType>))] public enum ActorType Fields [WireName("ServiceAccount")] ServiceAccount = 1 The server's ServiceAccount value. [WireName("System")] System = 2 The server's System value. [WireName("")] Unknown = 3 A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list. Its wire spelling is the empty string, which no server value is: carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than silently written as a spelling it never used. Fifteen of these enums appear in request bodies, which is what makes that distinction worth having. This is the FAPI "one switch". FAPI 2.0 is not a single feature but a bundle of constraints — mandatory PAR, mandatory PKCE with S256, mandatory strong client authentication, mandatory sender-constrained tokens, and a refusal of every relaxation the base specs permit. Encoding them as one profile rather than a dozen independent booleans means an operator cannot register a client that is nearly FAPI, and a reviewer can answer "is this client financial-grade?" by reading one field. The same philosophy as the rate-limit postures: ordinary clients see no behaviour change at all, because Standard is the serde default and every row written before schema v38 decodes to it. [JsonConverter(typeof(WireEnumConverter<ClientProfile>))] public enum ClientProfile Fields [WireName("fapi2")] Fapi2 = 1 The server's fapi2 value. [WireName("standard")] Standard = 0 The server's standard value. [WireName("")] Unknown = 2 A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list. Its wire spelling is the empty string, which no server value is: carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than silently written as a spelling it never used. Fifteen of these enums appear in request bodies, which is what makes that distinction worth having. It is deliberately not the zero member — defaulting to it would make “the server said nothing” and “the server said something new” the same value. Remarks Each member carries the spelling the server uses on the wire via WireName, so the C# name can follow C# conventions without changing what is sent. An open enum. A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list decodes to ClientProfile.Unknown rather than failing the response it arrived in (§27.11 rule 1) — a closed enum turns the next value the server adds into a parse error on the whole list, taking down every record on the page over one field of one of them. A switch over these members needs an Unknown arm.

[JsonConverter(typeof(WireEnumConverter<FailurePolicy>))] public enum FailurePolicy Fields [WireName("fail_closed")] FailClosed = 0 The server's fail_closed value. [WireName("fail_open")] FailOpen = 1 The server's fail_open value. [WireName("")] Unknown = 2 A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list. Its wire spelling is the empty string, which no server value is: carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than silently written as a spelling it never used. Fifteen of these enums appear in request bodies, which is what makes that distinction worth having. It is deliberately not the zero member — defaulting to it would make “the server said nothing” and “the server said something new” the same value. Remarks Each member carries the spelling the server uses on the wire via WireName, so the C# name can follow C# conventions without changing what is sent. An open enum. A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list decodes to FailurePolicy.Unknown rather than failing the response it arrived in (§27.11 rule 1) — a closed enum turns the next value the server adds into a parse error on the whole list, taking down every record on the page over one field of one of them. A switch over these members needs an Unknown arm.

api/Axiam.Sdk.Management.Models.Permissi.summary: Enum PermissionEffect Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Management.Models Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll Whether a grant permits an action or refuses it (B1, deny-override). # Precedence Default deny -> an [PermissionEffect::Allow] grant permits -> a [PermissionEffect::Deny] grant refuses, and beats every allow, wherever either sits in the resource hierarchy. Deny wins; there is no most-specific-wins tie-break. That choice is deliberate and is argued in full in claude_dev/deny-override-design.md §2.1. The short version: deny-override buys one checkable property — adding a deny rule can never widen access, and can never be undone by adding allows — and most-specific-wins buys expressiveness at the cost of making "is X denied?" unanswerable without enumerating every other rule that might out-specify it. [PermissionEffect::Allow] is the default, so data written before this existed, and clients that send no effect, both mean "allow". No migration. [JsonConverter(typeof(WireEnumConverter<PermissionEffect>))] public enum PermissionEffect Fields [WireName("allow")] Allow = 0 The server's allow value. [WireName("deny")] Deny = 1 The server's deny value. [WireName("")] Unknown = 2 A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list. Its wire spelling is the empty string, which no server value is: carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than silently written as a spelling it never used. Fifteen of these enums appear in request bodies, which is what makes that distinction worth having. It is deliberately not the zero member — defaulting to it would make “the server said nothing” and “the server said something new” the same value. Remarks Each member carries the spelling the server uses on the wire via WireName, so the C# name can follow C# conventions without changing what is sent. An open enum. A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list decodes to PermissionEffect.Unknown rather than failing the response it arrived in (§27.11 rule 1) — a closed enum turns the next value the server adds into a parse error on the whole list, taking down every record on the page over one field of one of them. A switch over these members needs an Unknown arm.

The window exists so an erasure triggered by mistake, or under coercion, can be undone — POST /api/v1/auth/account/delete/cancel works for exactly this long. It was fixed at 30 days in the handler, which meant the "cancel a pending deletion" control in the admin UI referred to a duration no operator could see or change. Shorter is the more restrictive direction, so a tenant may lower it and not raise it: it is time spent holding data the subject has already asked to have erased, and GDPR Art. 17(1) asks for that to be "without undue delay". The upper bound of 90 days is where Art. 12(3)'s one-month response deadline plus its two-month extension for complex cases runs out; anything past 30 wants a reason recorded. api/Axiam.Sdk.Management.Models.ReactorM.summary: Enum ReactorMode Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Management.Models Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll How a reactor participates in an event. [JsonConverter(typeof(WireEnumConverter<ReactorMode>))] public enum ReactorMode Fields [WireName("intercept")] Intercept = 0 The server's intercept value. [WireName("listen")] Listen = 1 The server's listen value. [WireName("")] Unknown = 2 A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list. Its wire spelling is the empty string, which no server value is: carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than silently written as a spelling it never used. Fifteen of these enums appear in request bodies, which is what makes that distinction worth having. It is deliberately not the zero member — defaulting to it would make “the server said nothing” and “the server said something new” the same value. Remarks Each member carries the spelling the server uses on the wire via WireName, so the C# name can follow C# conventions without changing what is sent. An open enum. A value this SDK’s copy of the spec does not list decodes to ReactorMode.Unknown rather than failing the response it arrived in (§27.11 rule 1) — a closed enum turns the next value the server adds into a parse error on the whole list, taking down every record on the page over one field of one of them. A switch over these members needs an Unknown arm.

[PermissionEffect::Allow] is the default, so data written before this existed, and clients that send no effect, both mean "allow". No migration. PgpKeyAlgorithm Key algorithm for OpenPGP keys. PgpKeyPurpose The purpose of an OpenPGP key. PgpKeyStatus Status of an OpenPGP key. ReactorMode How a reactor participates in an event. ScimTokenStatus Why a token is or is not currently usable — for display only. The authentication path never surfaces this distinction on the wire. SettingsScope Whether a settings row belongs to an organization or a tenant. TenantKind What a tenant is, as distinct from what state it is in. Reserved rather than inferred: an organization has exactly one tenant of kind [Self::Organization], enforced by a unique index rather than by convention. Deriving it from a magic slug or from "the oldest tenant" would make the organization scope something an operator could rename or delete by accident, and it is the scope the super-admin lives in. TenantStatus Lifecycle status of a tenant. A Suspended tenant remains stored and its data isolated, but is treated as administratively disabled. New tenants are Active by default. UnknownAaguidAction What to do with an AAGUID that has no MDS entry (i.e. FIDO Alliance has no metadata for it — not necessarily malicious, MDS coverage is incomplete for some legitimate authenticators). UserStatus The UserStatus values the server uses.

Search { get; } Property Value string Remarks Matched case-insensitively against the identifying fields of whatever is being listed — a name or username, plus the record id, so a UUID out of a log line can be pasted in as-is. Total then counts matches, not rows, which is what lets a pager built on it show a page count belonging to the result set it is paging. A term that is empty or all whitespace is treated the same way: a search box that fires on every keystroke sends one the moment it is cleared, and "rows containing the empty string" is a different question from "all rows". The server caps the term's length; this SDK deliberately does not re-implement that cap, because a client-side truncation the server would not have made is a silently different query. Throwing fails the whole response, so one field of one record the caller did not ask about would take down an entire page — including the records it did ask for. It never silently maps to the zero member, which is the trap this used to avoid by throwing: reading "suspended" as whatever happens to be declared first would turn a new state into a wrong one, and on this surface those states gate access. Unknown is a state of its own, and its wire spelling is the empty string — which no server value is, so carrying an unrecognised value back into an update is refused by the server rather than written as a spelling it never used. An enum with no Unknown member still throws, so this cannot quietly change behaviour for a hand-written enum that never opted in. api/Axiam.Sdk.Opaque.LoginExchange.html.summary: Class LoginExchange Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Opaque Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll One in-flight login (CONTRACT.md §23). public sealed class LoginExchange : OpaqueExchange, IDisposable Inheritance object OpaqueExchange LoginExchange Implements IDisposable Inherited Members OpaqueExchange.Dispose() object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Properties Ke1 The hex KE1 to send to login/start. public string Ke1 { get; } Property Value string Methods Finish(char[], string, KsfParams) Opens the envelope, producing KE3. public string Finish(char[] password, string ke2, KsfParams ksf) Parameters password char[] The account password; every copy this SDK makes is cleared, but not the caller's. ke2 string The server's hex KE2. ksf KsfParams The key-stretching function the server named. Returns string The hex KE3 to send to login/finish. Remarks A failure here is the whole of the client's authentication check, and covers both halves of the mutual authentication: the envelope only opens under the right password, and KE2's MAC only verifies if the server actually holds the record. Nothing may be sent afterwards (§23.4 rule 7). That case is an AuthError, unlike every other null return in this namespace. The distinction is the point: a wrong password, an account that does not exist and a server that does not hold the record are indistinguishable by design and are all authentication failures, whereas a key-stretching function this build cannot perform is a configuration problem, and reporting it as "invalid password" would send an operator looking in the wrong place. Exceptions AuthError The envelope did not open, or KE2 did not verify. NetworkError The exchange is already spent, or the key-stretching function is one this SDK cannot ask for.

api/Axiam.Sdk.Opaque.OpaqueEnrollment.ht.summary: Class OpaqueEnrollment Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Opaque Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll The opaque object CONTRACT.md §23 defines: a registration record and the server-issued session handle that identifies the exchange it came from. public sealed record OpaqueEnrollment : IEquatable<OpaqueEnrollment> Inheritance object OpaqueEnrollment Implements IEquatable<OpaqueEnrollment> Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The server cannot build this — it never sees the plaintext — so any request that sets a password has to carry it: POST /api/v1/users, /auth/password/change, /auth/reset/confirm and /admin/bootstrap. Note what is not here. The SRP enrolment this replaces carried a salt, a group and a full set of KDF costs, and required the account's canonical username — passing an email produced a verifier no login could ever satisfy, and renaming a user invalidated their verifier outright. A record binds to a credential identifier the server chooses, and the key-stretching parameters are the server's, so there is nothing here a caller can get wrong. api/Axiam.Sdk.Opaque.OpaqueExchange.html.title: Class OpaqueExchange | AXIAM .NET SDK
api/Axiam.Sdk.Opaque.OpaqueExchange.html.summary: Class OpaqueExchange Namespace Axiam.Sdk.Opaque Assembly Axiam.Sdk.dll One in-flight OPAQUE exchange, owning a native state handle. public abstract class OpaqueExchange : IDisposable Inheritance object OpaqueExchange Implements IDisposable Derived LoginExchange RegistrationExchange Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Remarks The handle is single-use: the library consumes it in Finish whether that succeeds or fails. This class takes it out of a one-shot slot, so a second Finish raises a .NET exception rather than handing a dangling pointer across the ABI. IDisposable and a finalizer, in that order of preference: using releases an abandoned exchange deterministically, and the finalizer catches a caller who started a login and never completed it. Both go through the same one-shot slot, so neither can double-free. Methods Dispose() Releases the exchange if it was never finished. Idempotent, and a no-op once Finish has spent the handle. public void Dispose() ~OpaqueExchange() Releases an exchange the caller abandoned without disposing it. protected ~OpaqueExchange()
